lessons.title: Determine the Volume of Rectangular Prisms
lessons.objective: I can find the volume of a rectangular prism with whole-number edges using length × width × height.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my work using the words volume, rectangular prism, cubic units, and edge.

concept.heading: How do we find the volume of a box?
concept.intro: Volume is how much space is inside a 3D shape. For a rectangular prism (a box), volume = length × width × height, measured in cubic units.
concept.keyIdea: Volume of Rectangular Prisms (Whole Numbers). Formula: V = Length × Width × Height = Base Area × Height (V = l · w · h = B · h). 1. Identify the length, width, and height of the box. 2. Multiply base area (l × w) by height (h). 3. Label answer in cubic units (e.g. in³, cm³, ft³)

worked.title: Watch me
lines: My time capsule box is 6 long, 4 wide, and 3 tall. I write the formula: V = length × width × height.
I put in the numbers: V = 6 × 4 × 3.
First I multiply two of them: 6 × 4 = 24.
Then I multiply by the last one: 24 × 3 = 72.
So the volume is 72 cubic units. I use cubic units because volume fills space in 3 directions.
linesEs: Mi caja de cápsula del tiempo mide 6 de largo, 4 de ancho y 3 de alto. Escribo la fórmula: V = largo × ancho × alto.
Entonces el volumen es 72 unidades cúbicas. Uso unidades cúbicas porque el volumen llena el espacio en 3 direcciones.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Now a smaller box: 5 long, 2 wide, 2 tall. What formula do we use?
Let's put in the numbers: V = 5 × 2 × 2. What is 5 × 2?
We got 10. Now multiply 10 × 2. What is the volume?
Yes, V = 20 cubic units. Don't forget the cubic units!
linesEs: Ahora una caja más pequeña: 5 de largo, 2 de ancho, 2 de alto. ¿Qué fórmula usamos?
Nos dio 10. Ahora multiplica 10 × 2. ¿Cuál es el volumen?
Sí, V = 20 unidades cúbicas. ¡No olvides las unidades cúbicas!

vocabulary.definition: The number of unit cubes inside a rectangular prism. Formula: V = l × w × h.
vocabulary.example: V = l × w × h; 3 × 4 × 5 = 60 cubic units.

vocabulary.example: A box 3 × 2 × 4 holds 24 unit cubes, so V = 24 cubic units

vocabulary.definition: A solid box shape with six flat rectangle sides.

vocabulary.definition: The units used to measure space inside, like cubic inches.
vocabulary.example: A tiny cube that is 1 in × 1 in × 1 in = 1 in³ (one cubic inch)

vocabulary.definition: How long, how wide, and how tall a box is.

vocabulary.definition: A flat shape that folds up into a solid.
vocabulary.example: A cross-shaped pattern of 6 rectangles folds into a rectangular box

vocabulary.example: A cube has 12 edges — 4 along the top, 4 along the bottom, 4 vertical

vocabulary.definition: A cube that measures one unit on every edge.
vocabulary.example: Unit cubes fill a prism with no gaps.

lessons.title: Represent Three-Dimensional Figures in Two Dimensions
lessons.objective: I can find the surface area of a solid by using its net.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my work using the words surface area, net, face, and two-dimensional.

concept.heading: How do we find the surface area of a box?
concept.intro: Surface area is the total area of all the flat faces of a solid. A net unfolds the box flat so you can see and add all 6 faces. The answer uses square units.
concept.keyIdea: Representing 3D Solids with Nets. 1. A net is a 2D flat pattern that folds into a 3D solid without overlapping. 2. Rectangular prism net has 6 rectangular faces in 3 congruent opposite pairs. 3. Surface Area is the total sum of the areas of all flat faces on the net

worked.title: Watch me
lines: My box is 8 in. long, 5 in. wide, and 3 in. tall. I unfold it into a net and see 3 pairs of faces.
Top and bottom: each is 8 × 5 = 40, and there are 2 of them, so 2 × 40 = 80.
Front and back: each is 8 × 3 = 24, so 2 × 24 = 48.
Left and right: each is 5 × 3 = 15, so 2 × 15 = 30.
I add all the pairs: 80 + 48 + 30 = 158. The surface area is 158 in².
linesEs: Mi caja mide 8 pulg de largo, 5 pulg de ancho y 3 pulg de alto. La desdoblo en una plantilla y veo 3 pares de caras.
Arriba y abajo: cada una es 8 × 5 = 40, y hay 2, así que 2 × 40 = 80.
Frente y atrás: cada una es 8 × 3 = 24, así que 2 × 24 = 48.
Izquierda y derecha: cada una es 5 × 3 = 15, así que 2 × 15 = 30.
Sumo todos los pares: 80 + 48 + 30 = 158. El área de superficie es 158 pulg².

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Now a smaller box: 4 long, 3 wide, 2 tall. How many pairs of faces does it have?
Top and bottom: 4 × 3 = 12, times 2 = 24. Front and back: 4 × 2 = 8, times 2 = 16.
Left and right: 3 × 2 = 6, times 2 = 12. Now add 24 + 16 + 12. What is the surface area?
Yes, SA = 52 in². Remember to use square units.
linesEs: Ahora una caja más pequeña: 4 de largo, 3 de ancho, 2 de alto. ¿Cuántos pares de caras tiene?
Arriba y abajo: 4 × 3 = 12, por 2 = 24. Frente y atrás: 4 × 2 = 8, por 2 = 16.
Izquierda y derecha: 3 × 2 = 6, por 2 = 12. Ahora suma 24 + 16 + 12. ¿Cuál es el área de superficie?
Sí, 52 pulg². Recuerda usar unidades cuadradas.

vocabulary.definition: The total area of all the faces of a solid. A net unfolds the solid flat so you can see every face and add their areas.
vocabulary.example: A box with 6 faces: 2(8×5) + 2(8×3) + 2(5×3) = 158 square units

vocabulary.definition: The total area of all the flat sides of a solid.
vocabulary.example: A box 6 × 4 × 2: SA = 2(24) + 2(12) + 2(8) = 88 in² — like wrapping paper needed

vocabulary.definition: A flat shape that folds up into a solid.
vocabulary.example: Cut along the edges of a cereal box and unfold it flat — you see all 6 faces

vocabulary.definition: One flat side of a solid shape.
vocabulary.example: A rectangular prism has 6 faces: top, bottom, front, back, left, right

vocabulary.definition: A flat shape with length and width, but no thickness.
vocabulary.example: A rectangle drawn on paper is 2D — it has length and width but no depth

vocabulary.definition: The line where two flat sides of a solid meet.
vocabulary.example: A cube has 12 edges — the lines where two flat faces connect

vocabulary.definition: A solid with one base and triangular sides that meet at a point.
vocabulary.example: A square base with 4 triangles.

vocabulary.definition: A corner point where edges meet.
vocabulary.example: A cube has 8 vertices.

support.prompt: What is the volume of a rectangular prism with l = 7 in, w = 3 in, h = 4 in?
support.explanation: V = l × w × h = 7 × 3 × 4 = 84 cubic inches.
feedback: Add 7 + 3 instead of multiplying? Volume uses multiplication of all three edges.
Multiply all three dimensions: 7 × 3 × 4, not 7 × 3 ÷ 2.
Square inches (in²) measure area, not volume. Volume is cubic (in³).
hints: Notice the three edge lengths: l = 7 in, w = 3 in, h = 4 in. Volume asks how much space fills the whole box.
Use the volume formula V = l × w × h, and remember volume is measured in cubic units (in³).
Start with 7 × 3 = 21 for the base, then multiply that result by the height, 4 inches.

support.prompt: A time capsule box has a volume of 120 cm³. Its length is 10 cm and width is 4 cm. What is its height?
feedback: Did you use the formula h = V ÷ (l × w) correctly?
Check your division. 120 ÷ (10 × 4) = 120 ÷ 40 = ?
Verify: 10 × 4 × ? = 120. What number works?
hints: You already know the volume (120 cm³) and two edges (10 cm and 4 cm). The height is the missing piece.
Work backward: since V = l × w × h, divide the volume by the base area (length × width) to find the height.
First find the base area: 10 × 4 = 40 cm². Then figure out what number times 40 gives 120.

support.prompt: Which unit is used for volume?
support.explanation: Volume measures 3D space, so it uses cubic units like in³. Square units (in²) are for area, and inches are for length.
feedback: Square inches measure area (2D), not volume (3D). Volume uses cubic units.
Inches measure length, not volume. Volume is always cubic units.
Degrees measure angles, not volume. Look for cubic units.
hints: Re-read each unit and think dimensions: volume fills 3D space — length, width, AND height.
Match the exponent to the dimensions: 2D area uses square units (²), so 3D volume needs one more dimension.
Picture stacking little cubes inside a box. Each cube is 1 in × 1 in × 1 in — which unit describes a cube like that?

steps: Dimensions: A time capsule box is 4 long, 3 wide, and 5 tall
support.explanation: The student only multiplied the length and width and forgot the height. That gives the area of one face, not the volume. Multiply all three edges: V = 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 cubic units.
hints: Look at the Calculate step. How many edges did the student multiply?
Volume needs all three edges: 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 cubic units, not just 4 × 3 = 12.

support.prompt: A rectangular prism has l = 6 in, w = 4 in, h = 2 in. What is its surface area?
feedback: Remember each face has a matching opposite face — double the sum of the three face areas.
That's the volume — surface area needs the sum of all six face areas, not length × width × height.
Check the units — surface area covers a flat surface, so it needs square units, not cubic.
hints: Surface area covers all 6 faces of the 6 × 4 × 2 box — it's not the same as the space inside.
Use SA = 2lw + 2lh + 2wh: find the three different face areas, double each, and add.
Start with the top face: 6 × 4 = 24 in². Then find 6 × 2 and 4 × 2 before doubling and adding.

support.prompt: How many faces does a rectangular prism have?
support.explanation: A rectangular prism has 6 faces: top, bottom, front, back, left, and right.
feedback: Don't forget the top and bottom — a box has faces all around it, not just the sides.
That's the number of corners (vertices), not the number of flat faces.
That's the number of edges, not the number of flat faces — count the flat surfaces instead.
hints: Picture a cereal box in your hands. Turn it: there's a front, a back, two sides, a top, and a bottom.
Count faces in opposite pairs — every face on a rectangular prism has a matching partner across from it.
Count the pairs: top/bottom is one pair, front/back is another, left/right is the third. Multiply pairs by 2.

support.prompt: Surface area is measured in which type of unit?
support.explanation: Surface area measures flat surfaces, so it uses square units. Volume uses cubic units.
feedback: Cubic units measure 3D volume, not a flat surface — surface area needs a different kind of unit.
Linear units only measure length in one direction — surface area covers a flat region, needing two dimensions.
Every measurement needs a unit — think about what kind of unit matches a flat, two-dimensional surface.
hints: Surface area measures the flat covering on the outside of a solid — like wrapping paper.
Flat 2D measurements use square units. Save cubic units for filling space and plain units for length.
Imagine covering one face with 1-inch squares. Each square is 1 in² — that's the kind of unit surface area counts.

support.prompt: Spot the Mistake — A Counted Face Was Skipped
steps: Read: A time capsule box from the net is l = 6 in, w = 4 in, h = 2 in. Find the surface area.
Label the faces: Top/Bottom: 6×4 = 24, Front/Back: 6×2 = 12, Left/Right: 4×2 = 8
Add the faces: SA = 24 + 24 + 12 + 8 + 8 = 76 in² (only one front/back face counted)
support.explanation: The student only counted one 12 in² front/back face. The net shows both a front AND a back, so both 12 in² faces must be added. Correct: SA = 24 + 24 + 12 + 12 + 8 + 8 = 88 in².
hints: Count the faces on the net — a box should have 6, not 5.
The front face (12 in²) has a matching back face (12 in²). Add both.

support.prompt: Predict the volume for these settings. Give the answer in cubic units. Round to four decimal places if needed.
support.explanation: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. One layer has 12 cubes; 2 layers give 24 cubes. Surface area is 52 square units.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

support.prompt: A rectangular package measures 4 by 3 by 2 cm. What is its volume in cubic centimeters?
support.explanation: One layer holds 4 × 3 = 12 unit cubes. Two layers hold 24.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

support.prompt: A prism net has four side faces and two rectangular bases. How many faces does the folded prism have?
support.explanation: Each part of the net becomes one face. Four side faces plus two bases gives six faces.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

core.prompt: Two storage bins: Bin A is 8 × 6 × 5 inches. Bin B is 9 × 4 × 7 inches. Which holds more and by how much?
core.explanation: Bin A: 8 × 6 × 5 = 240 in³. Bin B: 9 × 4 × 7 = 252 in³. Bin B holds 12 in³ more.
feedback: Calculate both volumes first: Bin A = 8 × 6 × 5 and Bin B = 9 × 4 × 7.
Which bin has the larger volume? Find the difference.
Check your arithmetic: 8 × 6 × 5 = ? and 9 × 4 × 7 = ?
hints: This is a two-part question: which bin holds more AND by how many cubic inches. You need both volumes first.
Find each volume with V = l × w × h, then subtract the smaller total from the larger to get the difference.
Start with Bin A: 8 × 6 = 48, then × 5. Next do Bin B: 9 × 4 = 36, then × 7. Compare the totals.

core.prompt: A rectangular prism has length 8 cm, width 5 cm, and height 4 cm. What is its volume?
feedback: Are you adding the dimensions? Volume multiplies all edges: length × width × height.
Multiply only two dimensions? All three must be multiplied: 8 × 5 × 4.
Check your multiplication: 8 × 5 = 40, then 40 × 4 = ?
hints: The prism's edges are 8 cm, 5 cm, and 4 cm. Volume means multiplying those edges, not adding them.
Apply V = l × w × h with all three numbers — leaving one out gives an area, not a volume.
Multiply 8 × 5 = 40 first, then multiply that result by the height, 4 cm.

core.prompt: A box has a volume of 72 in³. Its base is 6 in by 4 in. What is its height?
feedback: Find 6 × 4 first, then divide 72 by that result.
Multiply the dimensions instead of dividing? Use 72 ÷ (6 × 4).
Double-check: height × 24 = 72. What is height?
hints: You know the volume (72 in³) and the base (6 in by 4 in). Only the height is unknown.
Since volume = base area × height, divide the volume by the base area to work backward to the height.
First compute the base area: 6 × 4 = 24 in². Then ask: 24 times what equals 72?

steps: Dimensions: A capsule is 6 long, 5 wide, and 3 tall
core.explanation: The student multiplied the first two edges correctly (6 × 5 = 30) but then added the height instead of multiplying it. Every edge must be multiplied: V = 6 × 5 × 3 = 90 cubic units.
hints: Look at the Calculate step. Was the height added or multiplied?
Multiply all three edges: 6 × 5 × 3 = 90 cubic units, not 6 × 5 + 3 = 33.

core.prompt: A cube has edges of 5 cm. What is its surface area?
core.explanation: A cube has 6 identical faces. Each face: 5 × 5 = 25 cm². Total SA = 6 × 25 = 150 cm².
feedback: Square the edge length for one face's area first, then multiply by the number of faces.
That's the volume calculation (edge cubed) — surface area needs six face areas added together.
Check the units — a flat surface is measured in square units, not cubic.
hints: A cube's 6 faces are identical squares, each one 5 cm by 5 cm.
Find the area of one square face, then multiply by 6 — and keep square units (cm²).
One face is 5 × 5 = 25 cm². Now multiply that area by the number of faces, 6.

core.prompt: Spot the Mistake — One Pair Was Not Doubled
steps: Read: A time capsule box from the net is l = 7 in, w = 5 in, h = 4 in. Find the surface area.
Find each face pair: Top/Bottom: 7×5 = 35, Front/Back: 7×4 = 28, Left/Right: 5×4 = 20
Apply the formula: SA = 2(35) + 2(28) + 20 = 70 + 56 + 20 = 146 in² (left/right pair not doubled)
core.explanation: The student doubled the first two pairs but forgot to double the left/right pair. There are two 20 in² faces, so it should be 2(20) = 40, not 20. Correct: SA = 70 + 56 + 40 = 166 in².
hints: Every face pair has 2 matching faces — check that each area is multiplied by 2.
The left and right faces are both 5×4 = 20, so add 40 in², not 20 in².

core.prompt: Predict the volume for these settings. Give the answer in cubic units. Round to four decimal places if needed.
core.explanation: 5 × 3 × 2 = 30. One layer has 15 cubes; 2 layers give 30 cubes. Surface area is 62 square units.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

stretch.prompt: A shipping crate is 12 ft long, 3 ft wide, and 2 ft tall. How many 1-foot cubes exactly fill it?
stretch.explanation: The number of unit cubes equals the volume: 12 × 3 × 2 = 72 cubes.
feedback: Verify: 12 × 3 = 36, then 36 × 2 = ? cubes.
Not quite. The number of unit cubes equals the volume: 12 × 3 × 2 = ___ cubes.
Add dimensions or divide incorrectly? The volume (12 × 3 × 2) equals unit cubes.
hints: Each 1-foot cube takes up exactly 1 ft³, so the number of cubes equals the crate's volume in cubic feet.
Find the crate's volume with V = l × w × h — that total IS the number of unit cubes that fit.
Start with one layer: 12 × 3 = 36 cubes. Then multiply by the height, 2 ft, for the number of layers.

stretch.prompt: Two prisms have the same volume of 48 cm³. Prism A is 4 × 4 × 3. Prism B is 8 × 3 × h. What is h?
stretch.explanation: Prism A volume = 4 × 4 × 3 = 48 cm³. For Prism B, h = 48 ÷ (8 × 3) = 48 ÷ 24 = 2 cm.
feedback: Verify: 8 × 3 × h = 48. What value of h works?
Use the formula: h = Volume ÷ (length × width).
Not quite. Prism A volume = 4 × 4 × 3 = 48 cm³.
hints: Both prisms hold 48 cm³. Prism B gives you two edges (8 and 3) and hides the height h.
Use h = Volume ÷ (length × width): divide 48 by the product of Prism B's two known edges.
Multiply 8 × 3 = 24 first. Then find what number times 24 equals 48.

steps: Dimensions: l = 9 ft, w = 4 ft, h = 6 ft
stretch.explanation: 4 × 6 = 24, not 10. The student added instead of multiplied. Correct: V = 9 × 24 = 216 ft³.
hints: Check Step 3: what is 4 × 6?
4 × 6 = 24, not 10. The student added 4 + 6 instead of multiplying.

stretch.prompt: A box needs to hold exactly 60 cubic inches. Give three different sets of whole-number dimensions that work. Which set would make the box closest to a cube shape? Why might that matter?
stretch.frame: Option 1: ___ × ___ × ___. Option 2: ___ × ___ × ___. Option 3: ___ × ___ × ___. The ___ option is closest to a cube because ___. This matters because ___.
stretch.explanation: Any three whole numbers whose product is 60 work, such as 1 × 6 × 10, 2 × 5 × 6, and 3 × 4 × 5. Of those, 3 × 4 × 5 is closest to a cube because its edges are nearest to equal, and a cube-like box uses less material for its surface while holding the same 60 cubic inches.
hints: You need three DIFFERENT whole-number triples that multiply to exactly 60, like l × w × h = 60.
Start with a factor pair of 60 (like 6 × 10), then split one factor into two numbers to make a triple.
Try 60 = 6 × 10, then break the 10 into 2 × 5 for one triple. Then hunt for triples whose numbers are closer to equal.

steps: Dimensions: l = 10 in, w = 4 in, h = 3 in
stretch.explanation: The student forgot to multiply the last face pair by 2. It should be 2(4×3) = 24, not 12. Correct: SA = 80 + 60 + 24 = 164 in².
hints: Check Step 3: how many times does each face pair appear?
Each face pair has 2 matching faces. The student only counted one left/right face.

stretch.prompt: Two boxes have the same volume of 60 in³. Box A is 5 × 4 × 3. Box B is 10 × 6 × 1. Which box uses less wrapping paper (has less surface area)? Show your calculations and explain why a more cube-like shape might use less material.
stretch.frame: Box A: SA = 2(___) + 2(___) + 2(___) = ___ in². Box B: SA = 2(___) + 2(___) + 2(___) = ___ in². Box ___ uses less wrapping paper because ___.
stretch.explanation: Both boxes hold 60 in³, but wrapping paper is measured by surface area. Box A: 2(20) + 2(15) + 2(12) = 94 in². Box B: 2(60) + 2(10) + 2(6) = 152 in². Box A uses less paper because its dimensions are closer to a cube — flattening the same volume into 10 × 6 × 1 creates two huge 60 in² faces and a lot of extra covering.
hints: Both boxes hold 60 in³, but wrapping paper depends on SURFACE AREA — the outside covering, not the inside space.
Compute SA = 2lw + 2lh + 2wh for each box, then compare the two totals before you explain.
Box A first: faces are 5×4 = 20, 5×3 = 15, and 4×3 = 12. Double each and add, then repeat for Box B's faces.
